title: CSS Superpower: Unlocking the Magic of Container Queries
description: Components that respond to the space they sit in rather than the viewport, and the one declaration people forget to add.
content:
I hit this on a dashboard where the same card appeared in a narrow sidebar, a two-column main area, and a full-width settings page. Media queries couldn't help. The card only knew the window was 1400px wide, so in a 240px sidebar it still rendered a 2rem title across two lines. I shipped a wrapper div and a resize observer instead.

Container queries let a component ask about the box it sits in rather than the window.

What are Container Queries?

A media query asks how big the viewport is. A container query asks how big this element's parent is.

You opt a parent in as a container, then query it:

The container-type: inline-size line is the part I forget. Without it the @container block silently does nothing.

What Changes

  • Components respond to their own space, so one card can work in a sidebar and in a wide column without knowing which it's in.
  • Design system components stop needing props like isNarrow, passed down from a page that happens to know the layout.
  • You can drop the wrapper divs and JS resize listeners you may have added to fake this.

Widgets and sidebars can rearrange themselves when they run out of room.

Where I Use Them

  • Reusable UI components: buttons, cards, or widgets that need to work in more than one layout.
  • Dynamic grids: items that reflow when a column narrows, which happens constantly once users start dragging the window.
  • Complex layouts: sidebars and tool panels where font size or orientation should follow the panel width.

Real-World Example

A product card that stacks when it's cramped and goes horizontal when it has room:

In a tight sidebar it stacks. On a roomy page the image moves to the side. Same markup, same CSS.

Beyond Width

Width is the common case, but @container can query height and other container features too. Support is good enough now that I reach for container queries first when styling a component in isolation.

If one of your components keeps breaking in a narrow column, that's the one to convert first.

title: CSS Anchor Positioning: No More JavaScript Tooltips
description: Attach a tooltip or dropdown to another element in CSS, with fallback positions when the preferred side has no room.
content:
I've shipped the same tooltip logic in three codebases: measure the trigger with getBoundingClientRect(), place the panel, re-measure on scroll and resize. It works until someone puts the trigger in a scrolling container, and the panel drifts from the button.

Anchor positioning moves all of that into CSS.

What Is Anchor Positioning?

One element becomes the anchor. A second declares it's positioned against it.

The translate: -50% pulls the tooltip back by half its width, since anchor(center) aligns left edges. Miss it and the tooltip sits 40px right.

What It Replaces

Tooltips and dropdowns stop needing a positioning library. The browser tracks the anchor through scrolling, so the panel follows the button instead of drifting away from it. And position-try gives you fallback positions when the preferred direction has no room.

Most of the bugs in my old tooltip code were scroll bugs.

The position-try Fallback System

You define a few alternatives and the browser uses the first that fits. A tooltip that would overflow the bottom flips above the button:

You can list several fallbacks; the browser tries them in order. I haven't tested many at once.

Real-World Use Cases

  • Tooltips and popovers: the example everyone starts with.
  • Select dropdowns: custom selects that open near their trigger.
  • Context menus: right-click menus anchored to a zero-size element at the cursor.
  • Floating labels: labels that stay attached to their inputs.

Minimal Working Example

The tooltip uses position: fixed rather than absolute. With popovers, that's usually the version that behaves.

Browser Support

As of early 2025, anchor positioning is available in Chrome 125+ and Edge 125+. Firefox and Safari are still implementing it, so gate the CSS with @supports (anchor-name: --x) and keep the old solution as a fallback.

Worth adopting, but I'd keep the JS fallback in production for now.

title: Animating height: auto Is Finally Possible
description: interpolate-size and calc-size() remove the oldest hack in CSS. How they work, where they still fall short, and the fallback I keep using.
content:
I once shipped an accordion with max-height: 999px and a 300ms transition. It looked right until someone opened a panel with more text than the others: the animation finished long before the height did, then the panel jumped the last two hundred pixels. I spent an afternoon tuning the duration against the longest possible content, which is not a solution so much as a bet that the content never changes.

The root cause is obvious once you see it. auto is not a length, so there is nothing to interpolate. Two newer CSS features fix that properly.

The Grid Trick, Which Still Works

If you want something that works everywhere today, the 0fr to 1fr grid transition is the most reliable option:

Fractional units are interpolable, and auto never enters the picture. The inner wrapper is required, since the overflow has to be clipped by the grid item rather than the grid itself. It is a trick, but it is a trick that has held up for years.

interpolate-size

The direct fix is a single property that allows interpolation between a length and an intrinsic keyword:

Now this works:

The browser computes the auto height and animates to it. No magic number, no ResizeObserver, no layout thrash.

I scope it rather than putting it on :root:

The property changes how height, width, min-height, max-height and their logical equivalents behave, including how calc-size() resolves. App-wide it is easy to forget you enabled it and then spend an hour wondering why a flex item animates when it should snap. Scoped, the surprise stays local.

calc-size() When You Need More

calc-size() is the lower-level version. It takes an intrinsic size as a basis and lets you compute from it:

Inside the function, size refers to the basis, so you can add to it or multiply it:

This is how you animate to the content height while leaving room for a footer, without guessing at pixels.

Elements That Start Hidden

Height transitions usually pair with something appearing: a popover, a dialog, a toast. Those start in a state the browser has never painted, so there is nothing to transition from. @starting-style supplies that first frame:

The allow-discrete keyword is what keeps display: none and the top layer in the transition instead of removing them at frame zero. Without it the element disappears before the animation can run, and you get a flash with no visible motion.

Both Together

The accordion I use now keeps the grid version as the baseline and lets interpolate-size take over where it is supported:

No measuring, and the unsupported path is the one that already worked.

Support

interpolate-size and calc-size() are Chromium features. They are in Chrome and Edge now, and not in Safari or Firefox as far as I can tell from testing. @starting-style has wider support but is still recent enough to check before relying on it.

The grid trick stays the baseline; these properties are an enhancement. Writing the fallback first is not extra work here; it is the same markup with one extra @supports block, and it means the accordion behaves correctly in every browser instead of only in the one you tested.

title: CSS @property: Typed Custom Properties That Actually Animate
description: Typed custom properties make gradients and other complex values animatable, and give design tokens an actual type.
content:
I spent an afternoon trying to animate a gradient progress bar, wondering why the transition did nothing. The answer is that custom properties are stored as strings. The browser sees --stop: 20% and --stop: 80% as two unrelated pieces of text, so it can't work out the frames between them and the value snaps.

@property fixes that. It tells the browser what kind of value a property holds, which makes it animatable and gives the cascade a fallback for invalid values.

What Is @property?

@property registers a custom property with a type, an initial value, and an inheritance rule.

Once registered, the browser knows --hue is a number and can interpolate it. It can also reject values that don't match.

Animating Gradients (The Killer Use Case)

This doesn't animate. The gradient jumps from the start value to the end value:

Register it as a <percentage> and the same transition runs smoothly:

Supported Syntax Types

The syntax descriptor accepts these:

SyntaxExample value
<number>42
<integer>3
<length>16px, 1rem
<percentage>50%
<color>#ff0, oklch()
<angle>90deg
<length-percentage>calc(50% + 8px)
<transform-function>rotate(45deg)
*Any value

The wildcard brings back the string behaviour.

Typed Design Tokens

The other use is catching mistakes. A plain variable is a string, so nothing stops this until it looks wrong:

Registered, the property has a declared type and a fallback:

If someone writes --spacing-md: red, the declaration is invalid and the browser uses initial-value. I've only bothered for tokens that get animated or used in calc(), since registering everything is a lot of boilerplate.

Real Example: Animated Hue Rotation

The badge cycles through the hue wheel. Unregistered, it would jump from 0 to 360, the same colour, so it would appear to do nothing.

Browser Support

@property is supported in all modern browsers as of 2025 (Chrome 85+, Edge 85+, Firefox 128+, Safari 16.4+), so there's no need to guard it.

Small at-rule, narrow uses, but animated gradients come up often enough that I keep it.

title: A Fun CSS Fact: Meet the Magic of clamp()
description: One declaration instead of three breakpoints for type sizes, plus the viewport-unit catch that bites in narrow sidebars.
content:
First post, so I'll start with something small that I use constantly: clamp(). I picked it up while writing the same three media queries for every heading on a marketing site, adjusting font sizes at 480px, 768px, and 1200px, then doing it again on the next page.

What is clamp()?

clamp() takes a minimum, a preferred value, and a maximum. If the preferred value falls outside the range, the browser uses the nearest bound.

Paste it into dev tools and drag the window around to watch.

The Three Values

  • 1rem is the floor, so text stays legible on a phone.
  • 2.5vw is the preferred value. This is the part that scales with the viewport.
  • 2rem is the ceiling, past which text stops growing and the layout doesn't turn into a poster.

The size tracks the window in the middle of the range and holds steady at both ends. No breakpoints involved.

Where It Helps

  • Responsive font sizes: one declaration replaces a stack of media queries.
  • Spacings and gaps: section padding that doesn't look cramped on mobile or cavernous on desktop.
  • Width and height controls: a box that can grow and shrink but won't collapse or fill the screen.

Real-World Example

A heading that's readable in a narrow column and still reasonable on a wide monitor:

  • On small screens: 1.5rem
  • On big screens: up to 3rem
  • In-between: scales with the viewport width

The preferred value uses viewport units, so it ignores the container. Inside a narrow sidebar, 5vw on a 1400px window is 70px.

Other Lengths

clamp() works anywhere a length is accepted: shadows, margins, padding, border radii. Support is broad enough to skip the fallback.

If you've been writing breakpoints for type sizes, try a clamp.

title: Stop Hand-Picking Shades: color-mix() and Relative Colors
description: Derive hover states, borders and a whole palette from one brand colour in CSS, so a theme change stops being an afternoon of colour picking.
content:
The design file for a project I worked on had fourteen variations of the same blue. Four tints, four shades, a border blue, a focus blue, a disabled blue, two overlay blues. All hand-picked, all slightly inconsistent, and all of them wrong the week the brand colour changed.

I have stopped doing that. One token now, with the rest derived in CSS at runtime.

Mixing Two Colours

color-mix() blends two colours in a chosen interpolation space, with optional weights:

You do not have to make the percentages sum to 100. Leave one out and it becomes the complement, so the first line reads as 85% brand and 15% black.

The space matters. Mixing in srgb is what most colour pickers do, and it often lands on something muddy in the middle because sRGB interpolation takes a detour through the wrong part of the colour space. oklch and oklab are perceptually uniform, so a 15% step toward black looks like a 15% step. Pick one of the two and stay consistent; the difference between them is small enough that switching halfway through a palette is the real mistake.

Mixing toward transparent behaves differently enough to mention separately. color-mix() interpolates in premultiplied alpha space, so you get the brand colour at 20% opacity rather than a washed-out grey. Use white instead when you want an opaque tint and transparent when you want an overlay.

Changing One Channel

Mixing needs a second colour. When you want to move a single channel of one colour, relative syntax is the better tool:

oklch(from var(--brand) ...) says: convert this colour to oklch, then let me compute the channels from l, c and h. The three examples darken it, lighten and desaturate it, and desaturate it without touching lightness.

Once that clicks, a scale stops being a design task and becomes a formula:

Hue stays put across the whole ramp, which is the part hand-picked hex values almost never get right. Change --brand and the ramp follows.

The same syntax works in other spaces, with different channel names:

Channels keep their own types. In oklch, l and c are numbers, so calc(l - 0.1) is fine. In hsl, s and l are percentages, and calc(l - 10%) is what you need. Writing calc(l - 10) there produces an invalid colour and drops the declaration without an error you will notice.

A Button That Derives Everything

The pattern I use for interactive components:

The text colour is a near-white tinted by the button background, which keeps it cohesive without hard-coding a second value. The focus ring is the same hue at low alpha. Variants override one custom property and inherit everything else:

Hover, border, text and focus follow without a single extra selector.

Support and One Gotcha

Both features work in current browsers. If you need older ones, define a static value first and let the derived one override it:

An unsupported declaration is discarded and the fallback stays. But relative colours only resolve if the referenced value is a valid colour at computed-value time, so give --brand a default in var(): var(--brand, #4f46e5). Without it, the whole declaration fails, and the failure is silent.

The real payoff is not tidiness. When the brand colour changes, or dark mode needs different role tokens, or someone asks for a high-contrast variant, the work is redefining two or three values instead of auditing every component that hard-coded a shade.

title: CSS :has() — The Parent Selector That Changes Everything
description: Conditional styling based on descendants, siblings and form state, with the performance caveats that actually matter.
content:
For a long time CSS could only style an element from its ancestors or from siblings before it. :has() matches an element based on what it contains.

Basic Syntax

section:not(:has(*)) is the one I reach for most. CMS templates render a wrapper whether or not there is content in it.

Conditional Card Layouts

I had a grid where cards without images were shorter and the rows never lined up. Tying the layout to the content fixed it better than the modifier class did.

Form State Styling

Keep the server-side validation. pointer-events: none will not stop someone tabbing to the button and pressing Enter.

Sibling Selection via Parent

Step indicators are the obvious use: everything before the current step dims. Doing that from JavaScript meant a second pass over the list.

Quantity Queries

:has(:nth-child(3)) is true for three items and for thirty, so the last rule means "three or more". Exact counts past three get ugly.

Navigation Highlighting

body:has(dialog[open]) replaced a modal-open class in one of my projects. The scroll lock can't drift out of sync with the dialog now, which used to happen when a route change closed it without running cleanup.

Performance Considerations

Engines handle :has() better than they used to, but the selector is still re-evaluated when the DOM changes:

  • Avoid :has(*) on large lists, since it checks every child.
  • Prefer :has(> child) over :has(descendant) when the markup allows it.
  • Keep complex :has() selectors off :root and html.

Browser Support

  • Chrome 105+ (August 2022)
  • Safari 15.4+ (March 2022, which was first)
  • Firefox 121+ (December 2023)
  • Edge 105+ (August 2022)

If your audience includes an older Firefox ESR, treat :has() as an enhancement rather than load-bearing layout.

I have been deleting modal-open-style classes since Safari shipped this. Try it on one conditional layout first; stylesheet logic is easier to leave alone six months later.

title: CSS Logical Properties: Write Once, Support Every Writing Direction
description: Logical properties replace left, right, top and bottom with rules that follow the writing direction, which is what RTL support actually needs.
content:
Physical properties like margin-left and border-top assume text runs left to right and top to bottom. Set dir="rtl" on a page and a sidebar that looked fine starts pushing the wrong way. Change the writing mode and the layout is sideways.

Logical properties name the same edges relative to the writing mode instead of the screen, so you declare them once and they follow the text.

The Core Concept

Put left, right, top and bottom aside for a moment:

  • Inline axis: the direction text flows (horizontal in LTR, horizontal but reversed in RTL, vertical in some East Asian modes).
  • Block axis: perpendicular to text flow (vertical in most cases).
PhysicalLogical Equivalent
topblock-start
bottomblock-end
leftinline-start
rightinline-end

Margin and Padding

That is the whole change. inline-start resolves to left in LTR and right in RTL; same numbers, different mapping, nothing to override.

Shorthand Logical Properties

This replaces:

Converting our design system buttons was mostly deletion in the diff.

Width and Height

inline-size is width while text runs horizontally and height once it doesn't, so the same rule gives a different box under writing-mode: vertical-rl.

Borders and Inset

Positioned elements work the same way:

The inset shorthand is still ordered top, right, bottom, left. Mixing it with logical longhands in one rule is confusing, and I have done it.

Text Alignment

left still works, and an English-only site won't break either way. I use start so the next person doesn't assume the direction is fixed.

Full Reference Map

PhysicalLogical
margin-topmargin-block-start
margin-bottommargin-block-end
margin-leftmargin-inline-start
margin-rightmargin-inline-end
padding-toppadding-block-start
widthinline-size
heightblock-size
topinset-block-start
leftinset-inline-start
float: leftfloat: inline-start
text-align: lefttext-align: start

Browser Support

Logical properties have full support in all modern browsers. The shorthand forms like margin-inline and padding-block have been stable since 2021.

If you're starting a component library, use logical properties from the first commit. Retrofitting a codebase that mixes both is tedious, so existing sites are better off migrating a component at a time.

title: Stop Using HEX Colors: A Practical Guide to oklch()
description: Perceptually even colour, predictable lightness steps, wide-gamut output, and the contrast caveat that usually goes unmentioned.
content:
Picking a HEX color is guesswork. If a shade comes out too dark, you open a picker, nudge a channel, and hope the hue stayed put. oklch() separates lightness, chroma and hue, so you can change one without recalculating the other two.

What Is oklch?

oklch is OK (a perceptual correction) plus Lightness, Chroma and Hue. It sits on Oklab, where equal numeric steps look like equal perceptual steps. RGB and HSL don't have that property.

The syntax:

  • L — Lightness, 0 (black) to 1 (white). Also written as 0% to 100%.
  • C — Chroma (saturation), 0 (gray) to ~0.4 (vivid). Higher values are wider-gamut.
  • H — Hue angle, 0 to 360 (same wheel as HSL).

Why oklch Beats HSL

HSL's lightness channel lies to you. Two colors at the same value can look nothing alike:

Yellow at 50% glares; blue at 50% reads as a deep navy. In oklch, the same lightness value looks the same:

Perceptual lightness isn't contrast, though. Matching L values won't fix unreadable text, and I've shipped a palette like that.

Building a Color Palette

The useful part is generating a palette by varying one channel. Hold L and C, step the hue:

All eight read at roughly the same weight. The same set in HSL needs manual brightness fixes, especially around yellow and blue.

Generating Shades

Shades are the same trick on the lightness axis:

Chroma tapers at both ends so the light and dark steps don't look neon. That curve came from trial and error.

Wide Gamut Colors

oklch can describe colors outside the sRGB gamut, including P3 and Rec2020:

The browser maps that into whatever the display can show. On an sRGB monitor you get a muted green; on a P3 display the same value is noticeably more saturated. If the exact color matters on sRGB screens, keep the values inside the smaller gamut.

Using oklch in Tailwind CSS

Tailwind v4 defines its default palette in oklch. Custom colors are plain strings in the theme config:

Tools

  • oklch.com — interactive picker with P3 visualization.
  • Evil Martians oklch tool — palette generator.
  • Chromatic — VS Code extension with oklch support.

I haven't reached for a HEX value for a new palette in a while. Convert a handful of your tokens and see whether the shades you keep fighting with were badly chosen numbers.

title: CSS Scroll-Driven Animations: No JavaScript Required
description: Scroll-linked animation in CSS only, from progress bars to parallax, plus the jank that scaleX and a careless animation-range cause.
content:
Scroll-linked effects have usually meant an IntersectionObserver or a scroll listener with a requestAnimationFrame guard. CSS scroll-driven animations move that into the stylesheet.

Two Types of Scroll Timelines

  1. scroll() links progress to scroll position in a container.
  2. view() links progress to an element's visibility in a scroller.

You pick one per animation with animation-timeline.

Progress Bar With scroll()

A progress bar that fills as you scroll:

scroll(root block) is the document scroller on the vertical axis. Without both, the bar snaps to zero outside the range.

width triggers layout on every frame, so if the bar stutters, pin the element at full width and animate transform: scaleX() instead.

Reveal on Scroll With view()

Fade elements in as they enter the viewport:

entry 0% entry 40% starts as the top edge enters and finishes once 40% of the element is visible. On a tall card that is a long scroll; I ended up nearer 20%.

animation-range Reference

It picks which portion of the timeline drives the animation:

KeywordMeaning
entryElement entering the scroller
exitElement leaving the scroller
containWhile element is fully contained
coverFrom first pixel entering to last pixel leaving

cover is usually what people mean by "while it's on screen". contain counts only the stretch where it is fully inside the viewport.

Named Timelines for Complex Layouts

Use a named timeline when the scroller is not an ancestor:

The name has to be a custom identifier starting with --, or the declaration is dropped.

Parallax Effect

Parallax from a scroll listener is where I have seen the worst jank.

Browser Support

Chrome 115+, Edge 115+, Safari 18+ (fall 2024) and Firefox 132. Wrap it in @supports (animation-timeline: scroll()): an ignored animation-timeline leaves a normal timed animation, so cards fade in on load instead of on scroll.

Progress bars and fade-ins are where this has stuck for me. Neither needs a library.

title: CSS Subgrid: When Nested Layouts Finally Line Up
description: Subgrid lets a nested element share its parent's tracks. Where that saves markup, where the model bends, and what the fallback costs.
content:
I built a pricing page once where the three cards looked fine until the copy changed. One plan had a two-line description, so its price sat lower than the others, and the "Start trial" buttons ended up at three different heights. The fix was a pile of min-height values per breakpoint, which stayed correct for about a month. Then we translated the page and every card had different text again.

The cards were the same width. Their contents were not. That is the problem subgrid solves.

Why Nested Grids Ignore Each Other

A child grid starts from scratch. It computes its own tracks from its own content and knows nothing about the grid around it:

Three cards in a row, three grids inside them. Each .card sizes its own auto rows. If one title wraps, only that card's body moves down. The containers are siblings, but their rows never cooperate.

Sharing the Parent's Rows

You can tell the child to use the parent's track list instead of building one:

The title of every card now sits on row one, the description on row two, the button on row three. A long title makes that row taller for all three cards at once, which is what you wanted all along. No pixel values, no measuring, no wrapper elements.

Columns work the same way. A form is the other place I use this constantly:

Labels line up and inputs start at the same x position, while each field stays a self-contained component you can move around.

The Four Things That Catch People

You have to span the tracks first. grid-template-rows: subgrid only inherits rows the element already occupies. Without the matching grid-row: span 3, there is nothing to inherit and the declaration does nothing useful.

Subgrid does not add tracks. grid-template-rows: subgrid 100px is not a thing. The element joins the parent's sizing; it cannot insert a track of its own.

Gaps are the subgrid's decision. Gutters between the inherited rows come from the subgrid element's own gap, not the parent's. The parent's gap only applies between the subgrid and its siblings. I have gotten this backwards more than once.

Names have to be unique enough. Line names inherited from the parent keep working, which is handy, but two nested subgrids with the same names in the same place will confuse you faster than they will confuse the browser.

What the Fallback Costs

Support is broad enough now that a lot of sites can use subgrid without a plan B. When you do need one, @supports keeps it honest:

You lose cross-card alignment. Nothing breaks. For most card grids that is a small enough regression that I do not bother with a fallback at all; I only add it when the alignment is doing real work, like a pricing table where mismatched buttons look like a bug.

Where I Skip It

Subgrid is only useful when the nested element really does share a grid with its parent. A sidebar widget, a chart legend, a component dropped into an unrelated page: keep those as normal grids. Alignment you cannot see is not alignment worth inheriting.

For the pricing cards, the final CSS was about eight lines shorter than the version with min-height. That is the part I like. It removed code, and it kept working after translation.

title: Better Headlines Without JavaScript: text-wrap: balance and pretty
description: Two CSS declarations that fix stranded headline words and orphaned paragraph endings. When each one helps, and when it makes things worse.
content:
A headline that leaves one word alone on the last line is the kind of detail that makes a page look unfinished, even when nobody can say why. I used to fix it with a <br>, which held until the copy changed, or with a max-width nudge, which held until the viewport changed.

text-wrap handles both cases now, in CSS, with no measurement code.

Balancing Headings

text-wrap: balance tells the browser to spread words evenly across lines instead of filling each line greedily:

Instead of a three-line heading with a single word on the last line, you get two lines of similar length. The browser picks the break points; you just give it permission to try.

The algorithm is not free, so browsers treat it as a short-block optimization and fall back to normal wrapping past a few lines. That is why the usual advice is to put it on headings and leave body copy alone. The advice is right, though the reason is less about taste than about the browser quietly giving up on long blocks.

One more constraint. text-wrap: balance does nothing on inline elements, and nothing on a block whose width is determined by its own text. The block needs a resolved width first, otherwise there is nothing to balance against.

Fixing Paragraph Endings

Body text has a different problem. You are not trying to even out every line; you want to avoid a single word dangling at the end, and avoid the short final line that makes a paragraph look truncated.

pretty is cheaper and less ambitious than balance. It looks ahead a line or two and makes small adjustments so the paragraph ends well. It will not redistribute the whole block.

balance optimizes the shape of the block, pretty optimizes its last line. Use them on the wrong elements and you either waste work or get no visible change.

What I Ship

Two rules, applied globally, plus a measure cap:

The max-inline-size values matter more than the wrapping properties. A balanced heading stretched across a 1600px viewport produces lines so long that even distribution looks worse than a natural break. Constrain the measure first, then balance inside it.

nowrap Is in the Same Family

text-wrap also takes nowrap, which is the modern spelling of white-space: nowrap for the wrapping axis:

It is a shorthand for text-wrap-mode and text-wrap-style. You rarely need the longhands, but they are there when you want to be explicit about the difference:

Why It Is Safe to Add Today

Unknown keyword values are ignored, so older browsers keep wrapping text exactly as they always did:

That second declaration drops out, and nothing else changes. No @supports, no layout shift, no JavaScript. The worst case is the pre-2023 rendering, which is what most of the web still looks like.

Where It Does Not Help

Buttons and short labels are too short to balance. A heading inside a 200px sidebar can come out looking worse balanced than broken naturally, because there is not enough room for the algorithm to work with. And anything that must break at a specific word still needs   or a <br>.

Everything else gets the two declarations. This site has had them in its base stylesheet since the redesign, and I have not thought about a stranded headline word since.

title: View Transitions: Animate Between Pages Without an Animation Library
description: How the View Transitions API works, what the pseudo-elements give you, and the two mistakes that make it look broken.
content:
The first page transition I ever shipped was a pair of CSS classes and a setTimeout. Fade the list out over 200ms, swap the DOM, fade it back in. It looked fine in a demo and terrible in use, because any click during those 200ms produced a flash of half-faded content. The user could outrun the animation, and there was no good way to stop them.

The View Transitions API exists because that problem is not solvable with a class and a timer. The browser takes a snapshot of the current state, runs your DOM update, snapshots the result, and animates between the two images. Interrupt it and it blends from whatever is on screen instead of starting over.

The Basic Call

That is a cross-fade of the whole page, and it already behaves better than most hand-rolled versions. If your update is asynchronous, return a promise and the browser waits:

Naming the Elements That Should Move

A cross-fade is fine. Moving things is the interesting part. Give an element a name and the browser treats the before and after versions as the same object:

In practice you set the name dynamically, because only one element can hold it at a time:

The avatar now travels from the list into the header. Two rules do most of the work here. Names have to be unique within each snapshot; duplicate names abort the transition, and the browser logs an error rather than falling back gracefully. And for a morph, both states need the name. If only the new state has it, the element fades in from nothing, which looks like a bug even though it is the documented behaviour.

The Pseudo-Elements

Every named element generates a small tree you can style:

group is the container that moves and scales. image-pair holds the two snapshots. The old and new pseudo-elements are the snapshots themselves, and the default cross-fade is just CSS you are allowed to replace. Splitting the durations like this is usually what makes a transition feel intentional rather than sluggish: the outgoing content can leave faster than the incoming content arrives.

Across Real Page Loads

For a multi-page site, one rule in both documents opts in:

The same view-transition-name values now work across navigations. No JavaScript, no router integration.

This is also where framework expectations go wrong. Client-side routing is not a document navigation. In the Next.js App Router, clicking a <Link> does not trigger this path, so @view-transition never fires and it looks like the feature is broken. You have to call startViewTransition around the router update yourself.

With React

React batches state updates, so the DOM may not have changed by the time your callback returns. flushSync forces the commit inside the snapshot window:

Use it here and nowhere else. Forcing synchronous rendering across the app undoes the scheduler for no benefit.

Motion Preferences

Transitions are decorative, so they should disappear when someone asks for less motion. The CSS version covers transitions you did not start yourself:

Or skip the call entirely:

What I Would Do Differently

Keep the durations short. Route transitions over 300ms feel slow on the fifth click, even if they looked elegant in review. Give different elements different names only when you actually want them to morph; a name on everything turns a page change into a fairground. And feature-detect the method rather than the browser, so Safari and Firefox get a plain, instant navigation instead of a broken one.

For the list-to-detail case, the version in this post replaced roughly forty lines of fade-in/fade-out state management. That is the strongest argument for it, more than the animation itself.

title: Native CSS Nesting Is Here: Ditch the Preprocessor
description: Native CSS nesting works in every current browser. The syntax, the `&` rules, and what still needs a preprocessor.
content:
Nesting selectors inside other selectors was the main reason I put up with Sass for years. Browsers handle it natively now, and there's no build step involved.

Basic Syntax

Which is the same as writing this:

The & Selector

& means the parent selector. You need it when you're appending to the parent rather than adding a descendant:

Bare .icon and & .icon compile to the same thing. I still write the second one when I mean a descendant, because it survives being moved out of the block during a refactor.

Media Queries Inside Selectors

@media, @supports and other at-rules nest too:

The responsive overrides stay next to the rule they change. In flat CSS the mobile version of a component ends up 400 lines below it.

Nesting and Specificity

A nested selector has the same specificity as the flat version. Nesting adds no weight:

Good news when porting Sass, less so if you hoped nesting would settle a specificity fight. It won't.

Key Difference From Sass: Interpolation

Native nesting has no equivalent of Sass selector interpolation:

If selectors have to be generated from a variable, a preprocessor or JavaScript is still the way.

Mixing With CSS Custom Properties

Custom properties and nesting go together well for component theming:

Overriding --bg on hover rather than background keeps the hover rule from having to know the base colour. Small thing, but it's the reason I started structuring themes this way.

Migrating From Sass

Most Sass nesting converts one-to-one. The differences worth knowing:

FeatureSassNative CSS
Basic nesting✅✅
& concatenation✅✅
@media nesting✅✅
Variables$var--var
Interpolation#{$var}❌ Not supported
Mixins@mixin❌ Not supported
Functionsdarken() etc.oklch(), color-mix()
Loops@each, @for❌ Not supported

If nesting and variables were the only Sass features a project used, native CSS covers it now.

Browser Support

All current browsers support it:

  • Chrome 120+ (December 2023)
  • Firefox 117+ (August 2023)
  • Safari 17.2+ (December 2023)
  • Edge 120+ (December 2023)

So the preprocessor can go, provided nothing else in the build depends on it. Fewer tools to keep current, and the CSS does the same job.

title: React 19 Hooks You Should Be Using in Next.js
description: useOptimistic, use(), useFormStatus and useActionState, with the placement rules and argument order that are easy to get wrong.
content:
React 19 shipped hooks built around Server Actions. These are the ones I reach for in Next.js, and where each has tripped me up.

useOptimistic: Instant UI Updates

useOptimistic holds a temporary UI state while an async operation is in flight. When it settles, React renders from the real state again.

The heart fills on the click, before the request finishes. If the action fails, the button returns to initialLiked. I hand-rolled that once.

use(): Consume Promises and Context

use() unwraps a Promise or Context value inside a component. It isn't a hook in the rules-of-hooks sense, so it can be called inside a condition or a loop.

Resolving a Promise

It doesn't fetch anything, which was my first wrong assumption. The promise has to exist already, usually created on the server and handed down. Without a Suspense boundary, the nearest parent catches the wait.

Reading Context

useFormStatus: Access Parent Form State

useFormStatus reads the pending state of the nearest parent <form>.

It has to be a child of the form. Call it in the component that renders <form> and pending stays false; that cost me an afternoon. It also lives in react-dom.

useActionState: Form Actions With State

useActionState (it was useFormState before the 19 release) keeps the value returned by a Server Action across submissions:

The Server Action returns State:

The argument order is easy to get backwards: previous state first, then the form data. Return the same shape on every path.

useTransition: Non-Blocking State Updates

useTransition marks updates as low priority so input stays responsive during async work. React 19 lets startTransition take an async function directly.

Typing keeps up while the request runs. Two responses can still land out of order, though. I've had to track a request id for that more than once.

When to Use Which

HookUse case
useOptimisticShow immediate feedback before server confirms
use()Unwrap promises passed from server; read context conditionally
useFormStatusDisable/style submit buttons based on form pending state
useActionStateManage form submission state and error/success messages
useTransitionKeep UI responsive during expensive updates

They're designed to work with Server Actions, so one in isolation rarely helps. Start with useOptimistic and useFormStatus if you have hand-rolled pending state to delete.

title: React Server Components: The Mental Model That Makes It Click
description: What `"use client"` actually marks, how server data reaches client components, and the serialization rule behind most RSC errors.
content:
Server Components have been stable in Next.js since v13, and people still bounce off them. Most of the confusion I've seen comes from one wrong assumption: that "use client" marks a component. It marks a boundary.

The Core Mental Model

Your component tree runs in two environments.

The server has the database, the filesystem and the secrets. It renders once per request and sends back HTML plus a description of the component tree the client can understand.

The client has browser APIs, event handlers and state. It receives that output and hydrates the parts that need to respond to a user.

The line between them is the "use client" directive. Everything above that line, toward the root, is a Server Component by default.

What Server Components Can and Cannot Do

Can:

  • async/await directly — no useEffect for data fetching
  • Access environment variables without exposing them to the client
  • Import Node.js modules (fs, crypto, database drivers)
  • Render other server components

Cannot:

  • Use useState, useEffect, or any React hooks
  • Attach event handlers (onClick, onChange)
  • Access browser APIs (window, document, localStorage)

The Right Way to Fetch Data

No API route, no client-side fetch. By the time the browser sees anything, the data is already markup. The next: { revalidate } option is Next-specific; the async component itself is plain React.

Passing Server Data to Client Components

Server Components can import and render Client Components, passing data as props. Props have to be serializable, which rules out functions and class instances.

Functions are the usual trip-up. Handing an onClick down from a Server Component fails, because it can't cross the wire, so the handler lives inside the Client Component.

The "Client Boundary" Rule

"use client" marks a boundary, not a single component. Everything imported by a Client Component is treated as client code, even if the file has no directive.

ServerPage (server)
└── ClientWrapper "use client" (client)
    └── SomeComponent (also client — even without "use client")

This is the reason to push "use client" as far down the tree as you can. I moved it down two levels in a docs layout once, just to keep the markdown renderer on the server, and the shipped bundle lost a chunk of parsing code. Data fetching and heavy logic stay on the server that way.

Server Actions: Mutations From the Server

Server Actions let you define server-side functions that Client Components can call:

No API route involved. Because the form posts to a real action, it also works before JavaScript has loaded.

Server Components render data into markup and Client Components add the interactivity on top. Keep "use client" low in the tree and let the server do the rest.

title: useDeferredValue: Keep Slow Lists Feeling Instant
description: What useDeferredValue actually defers, why it needs memoised children to do anything, and where a debounce is still the right tool.
content:
A search field filtering two thousand rows is a small performance problem with an outsized feel. Every keystroke re-renders the list, the input drops a frame or two, and the page starts to feel like it is thinking about whether to accept your typing.

The instinct is to debounce the query. That fixes the list and breaks the input, because now the characters you type appear late. useDeferredValue avoids both failures: the field updates immediately, and the expensive part catches up when the browser has a free moment.

The Shape of It

Two updates happen per keystroke. query updates synchronously and drives the input. deferredQuery lags, and React renders the list at a lower priority. If another keystroke arrives first, the pending render is thrown away and restarted with the newer value.

The query !== deferredQuery comparison is how you know a deferred render is in flight. I use it to dim the list slightly. A list showing results for the previous query looks broken if it is not marked as stale.

It Is Not a Debounce

These get conflated because they sound similar, but the mechanism is different in a way that changes when you should reach for each.

A debounce waits a fixed amount of time and then runs. useDeferredValue waits for React to have capacity, with no delay at all. If the browser is idle, the deferred render happens immediately after the urgent one. If the user keeps typing, the deferred work never finishes and never has to.

That makes deferred values good for render work and bad for network requests. There is no cancellation, no minimum interval, and no way to say "wait until they stop typing." For a fetch, debounce it, or abort the previous request.

Why It Sometimes Appears to Do Nothing

The hook lets React skip a subtree during urgent renders. It cannot skip a subtree that is not memoised, because the parent re-render drags the children with it:

Wrap it:

The same applies to the filtered array. Rebuild it inline and the new identity defeats the memo boundary on every urgent pass:

This is the part that makes people give up on the hook. Without the memo boundary there is nothing being deferred, and the behaviour looks identical to not using it.

The Second Argument in React 19

React 19 added an initial value:

It is the value used on the first render, before any deferred update has happened. The case that matters is when the initial value is expensive and arrives from a Server Component:

Without it, the first render includes the full dataset and blocks. Usually you want that on initial load; occasionally you want the shell first.

Deferred Value or Transition

They overlap enough that picking one is mostly about what you control. If the slow work comes from a value you do not own, defer the value. If you own the update, wrap it in startTransition and read isPending for the indicator.

useDeferredValueuseTransition
WrapsA value you consumeA state update you trigger
Pending signalvalue !== deferredValueisPending
FitsExpensive rendering of propsExpensive state changes

You can combine them, and occasionally a codebase needs both, but needing both in one component usually means the state should be split differently.

Where I Do Not Use It

Validation messages. A hint that lags 300ms behind the field reads as a bug, not as speed. Cheap lists, where the bookkeeping costs more than the render. And anything that must match the input exactly, like a live character count.

For the filtered list case, though, it is two lines and no timers, and the loading spinner I would otherwise have written never needs to exist.

title: What Web Design Actually Looks Like in Late 2026
description: Which trends made it into production this year, which are still stuck on award sites, and the CSS that separates the two.
content:
Trend reports mostly describe moodboards. This is about what I keep seeing in production sites, client work and code review: the decisions that have become defaults, the ones that only survive on award pages, and the CSS behind both.

Type got loud, layout got quiet

Display type is bigger and tighter than it was two years ago. Variable fonts, oxblood-red headlines, oversized serif wordmarks, letter-spacing pulled negative until it nearly touches. This is everywhere in 2026, and it is cheap to ship because fonts got better and clamp() removed the breakpoint math.

The structure under all that type went the other way. Fewer drop shadows, fewer rounded cards floating on gradients, more hairline rules and flat surfaces. The visual budget moved from decoration to typography, which is why so many current sites look like a well-set document with one enormous headline.

Balanced wrapping stops the headline leaving one word alone on the last line, which matters more now that the headline is 80px.

Bento grids grew up

The bento layout, a grid of mixed-size tiles, has been around long enough to stop being a trend and become a pattern. It survived because it holds genuinely different content: a screenshot here, a metric there, a quote in the tall cell. Apple's product pages did the popularising; everyone else did the copying.

What changed is the implementation. Two years ago most of these were hand-positioned divs with magic row spans. Now they are ordinary grids with a couple of spanning rules, and the tiles align internally with subgrid.

The pattern is also where sameness set in. When every SaaS homepage has the same five-tile composition with a dashboard screenshot in the big cell, the layout stops communicating anything. I have talked two clients out of it this year for exactly that reason.

Colour moved into OKLCH and got quieter

Token work is finally in the perceptual colour spaces. oklch() for palette definition, color-mix() for hover and border states, one loud accent against warm neutrals instead of four competing gradients. The muted palettes are partly a reaction to a decade of saturated purple, and partly practical: OKLCH keeps lightness consistent across a palette, so contrast survives a theme change.

The other half of this trend is texture. Fine grain over flat colour, paper-like backgrounds, barely-there noise. It reads as a rejection of the perfectly smooth gradient, and it costs about eight lines of CSS plus a small PNG.

Glass came back with a contrast bill

Translucent panels returned in force after Apple's Liquid Glass work, and the web version is backdrop-filter plus a semi-transparent background. It looks convincing on a bright hero image and falls apart on text-heavy content, where the panel has to sit over an unknown background.

The version that survives production has a solid fallback and a real background colour behind the blur:

The accessibility issue is real and routinely ignored: text at 4.5:1 over a solid surface drops below that once the surface is at 80% opacity and something dark scrolls underneath. If the panel contains body copy rather than a label, I use a near-opaque background and let the blur do the rest.

Motion became native or nothing

Almost none of the motion work I see now ships as a JavaScript animation library. Route changes use the View Transitions API, scroll effects use CSS scroll-driven animations, and entrance animations use @starting-style. The browser does the interpolation, which means it also respects prefers-reduced-motion without extra plumbing.

Durations shrank too. Two years ago a page transition was 400ms; now anything above 250ms feels like the site is thinking. The exception is scroll-linked motion, where the user controls the pace and duration is irrelevant.

What is fading is motion as decoration: parallax on every section, cards floating up on scroll, hover states that take 600ms to settle. That vocabulary now reads as dated, in the same way auto-playing carousels do.

AI became an interface, not a feature

The most visible change of the last year is structural. Chat is no longer a widget in the corner; it is the page. Search boxes turned into prompt boxes, empty states turned into suggested prompts, and the answer arrives as a streamed document with citations underneath.

Designing that well is mostly about states nobody used to design: the first token arriving, a partial answer that changes, a citation that might be wrong, a regenerate button, an escape hatch back to the normal UI. The sites that feel trustworthy show where the text came from. The ones that do not feel like a magic trick with a legal disclaimer.

There is a backlash, and it is aesthetically specific. The purple gradient, the sparkle icon, the generic 3D blob illustration, the assistant that greets you by name. Those have become the visual signature of low-effort AI product, and good teams are actively avoiding them.

Accessibility turned into a deadline

For European products, the European Accessibility Act became enforceable in June 2025. That moved accessibility from a quarterly aspiration to a procurement requirement, and it shows in the work: focus states designed rather than defaulted, target sizes checked, custom selects rebuilt because the old one could not be operated by keyboard.

WCAG 2.2's focus-appearance and target-size criteria did more for interface quality than most design trends this year, largely because they are testable.

What I am tired of

Scroll-jacking on marketing pages. Hero sections that are a stock photo plus a headline plus two buttons, indistinguishable from the next site. Cookie banners designed to be harder to dismiss than the thing they are asking about. Dashboards mocked up with fake numbers and no indication that they are fake. And the phrase "delightful" attached to a loading spinner.

None of those are new. They persist because they are easy, and because nobody gets performance-reviewed for removing an effect.

The through-line

The interesting shift is not a visual style. It is that the browser caught up. Layout, colour, motion and transitions that used to need libraries or build tooling are now a handful of declarations, which means design decisions and CSS decisions are the same conversation.

The sites I have liked most this year are the ones that used that to remove things: fewer effects, fewer dependencies, a tighter type scale, and one accent colour doing actual work.
